summary: Pulse Star is an evidence-traceable web platform designed for the "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars" challenge. Rather than relying on oversimplified "similarity percentages," Pulse Star evaluates an under-studied terrestrial candidate—Chandragup I Mud Volcano in Balochistan, Pakistan—against five established NASA/ESA Moon and Mars benchmarks (Atacama Desert, Haughton Impact Crater, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Craters of the Moon, and Río Tinto). Users can explore sites on an interactive multi-layer map with an offline WGS84 coordinate-grid fallback, compare locations across five independent qualitative rubric dimensions (Morphology, Geochemistry, EVA/Trafficability, Thermal Regime, and Subsurface Potential), inspect physical boundary limits such as Mars's 0.378 gravity ratio and ~6.1 mbar pressure, and export Markdown, JSON, and GeoJSON research dossiers.
details:
What Pulse Star Does & How It Works

Choosing Earth locations to test rovers, drills, and spacesuits for the Moon and Mars is often limited to a handful of famous sites, or relies on misleading single-number "similarity scores." Pulse Star solves this with a transparent, four-tab research and field-planning workflow:

1. Overview: Introduces the provisional hypothesis pairing Chandragup I Mud Volcano (Pakistan) with ~18,000 pitted cones in Acidalia Planitia (Mars) alongside five literature-backed Moon and Mars benchmarks.

2. Explore: Provides an interactive WGS84 map (Satellite Imagery, Topographic, OpenStreetMap, Dark Relief) plus a built-in offline vector coordinate-grid fallback for field teams working without internet access.

3. Compare: Evaluates sites across five independent qualitative dimensions (Morphology, Geochemistry, EVA/Trafficability, Thermal Regime, and Subsurface Potential) on a 0–100 ordinal rubric with zero composite averaging, explicit gravity (9.81 vs. 3.71 m/s², 0.378 ratio) and atmospheric pressure (~1013 vs. ~6.1 mbar) breakdown limits, 8-domain Field Operations profiles, risk matrices, and SOP checklists.

4. Evidence: Separates Dataset Identification, Geographic Coverage, Literature References, Basemap Inspection, and Independent Processing status, preserves unmeasured parameters strictly as null, and exports standalone Markdown (.md), JSON, and GeoJSON reports.

Tools, Software & Super Intelligence (SI) Transparency

Built as a zero-backend, single-file web application using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Leaflet, and Chart.js, developed on an iPad workflow and hosted via GitHub Pages (https://github.com/usman-system/pulse-star-nasa-space-apps-2026). Super Intelligence (SI) tools (Google Gemini) were used to assist with code generation, responsive UI structuring, and scientific literature synthesis; all claims, dataset provenance statuses, and unverified parameters were audited and explicitly disclosed in the app's Evidence ledger.

48-Hour Hackathon Scope & Future Roadmap

Within the 48-hour hackathon timeframe, development prioritized scientific validity, dataset provenance, and offline map reliability. Minor visual refinements—such as expanded Dark Relief tile styling and additional layout polish in the Compare view—are scoped for post-hackathon updates.
